terms.Branch:
A Git branch is a mutable reference, a small file under .git/refs/heads/ holding the object ID (40 hex characters for SHA-1) of a commit, called the tip. History is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of immutable, content-addressed commits; making a commit creates a node whose parent is the current tip and then moves the branch pointer forward. HEAD is normally a symbolic reference naming the checked-out branch, so a branch is a movable label, not a copy of files, and creating one costs a few dozen bytes.

In practice, git switch -c name creates and checks out a branch, and git branch -d refuses to delete one whose commits are not reachable from elsewhere unless forced with -D. Commits left unreachable after a deletion survive until garbage collection and can usually be recovered through the reflog.

Common confusion: a commit does not belong to one branch; it is merely reachable from zero or more tips. A tag is similar to a branch but never moves, and a detached HEAD points straight at a commit, so new commits are easily lost.
terms.Breadth-first search:
Breadth-first search (BFS) traverses a graph G = (V, E) from a source s using a first-in-first-out queue. It sets dist[s] = 0, then repeatedly dequeues a vertex u and, for each unvisited neighbour v, sets dist[v] = dist[u] + 1, records parent[v] = u and enqueues v. Vertices are therefore discovered in nondecreasing distance, so dist is the minimum number of edges from s. Time is O(V + E) with adjacency lists (O(V^2) with a matrix); space is O(V). Mark vertices as visited when enqueued, not when dequeued, or they can enter the queue many times.

Variants: multi-source BFS seeds the queue with several sources (for example the distance of every grid cell to its nearest wall); 0-1 BFS uses a deque for edge weights of 0 or 1; bidirectional BFS searches from both ends and cuts about b^d work to roughly 2·b^(d/2) for branching factor b and depth d. The frontier can reach O(b^d) memory, which is why iterative-deepening DFS is used when memory binds.

It does not give shortest paths in weighted graphs; use Dijkstra (non-negative weights) or Bellman-Ford.
terms.Byte-pair encoding:
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) was introduced as a compression scheme (Gage, 1994) and adapted to subword vocabularies for neural translation by Sennrich, Haddow and Birch (2016). Training: start with a base alphabet (characters, or the 256 byte values in byte-level BPE as used by GPT-2), count adjacent symbol pairs over a corpus weighted by word frequency, merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, append it to an ordered merge list, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches a target size V. Encoding a new string applies the merges in learned priority order, so tokenization is deterministic.

Details matter: a pre-tokenization step (often a regular expression splitting on whitespace, punctuation and digit runs) fixes the boundaries across which merges cannot occur. Byte-level BPE never produces unknown tokens. Larger V shortens sequences, cutting attention and generation cost, but enlarges the V×d embedding and output matrices and leaves rare tokens with poorly trained embeddings.

Related methods: WordPiece picks merges by likelihood gain; the Unigram model (Kudo, 2018) prunes a large vocabulary with EM and can sample alternative segmentations. BPE tokens are frequency artifacts, not morphemes.
terms.Calibration:
A probabilistic classifier is perfectly calibrated if, for every confidence level p, P(prediction is correct | stated confidence = p) = p. It is usually measured with a reliability diagram: bin predictions by confidence and compare each bin's mean confidence with its empirical accuracy. The summary statistic is expected calibration error, ECE = Σ_b (|B_b|/n) · |acc(B_b) − conf(B_b)|. ECE depends on the binning and usually covers only the top label.

Calibration is not accuracy: always predicting the base rate is calibrated yet useless. Proper scoring rules such as the Brier score and log loss decompose into a calibration term plus a refinement (discrimination) term. Guo et al. (2017) showed modern deep networks are often overconfident and that temperature scaling, dividing logits by a scalar T fitted on a validation set, largely fixes it without changing the argmax. For language models, token probabilities of pretrained models have been reported as fairly well calibrated on multiple-choice questions, while post-training can worsen this; verbalized confidence is a separate, weaker channel.

Neighbours: conformal prediction gives coverage guarantees for prediction sets rather than calibrated probabilities.
terms.Capability threshold:
In frontier-AI safety frameworks (for example Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy and Google DeepMind's critical capability levels), a capability threshold is a pre-committed level of a specific, risk-relevant ability. It is paired with an if-then commitment: if a model reaches the level, defined safeguards must be in place before further scaling or deployment. Thresholds are written in terms of a threat model and counterfactual impact, for example meaningful uplift over what a person could do with ordinary internet tools, rather than a benchmark score.

Because the real capability cannot be observed directly, labs run evaluations with strong elicitation (scaffolding, tools, fine-tuning, repeated sampling) to bound it from above, and often set earlier warning triggers with a safety margin below the threshold. When results are ambiguous, a precautionary rule treats the threshold as crossed; Anthropic applied this logic to activate ASL-3 protections for Claude Opus 4. Failure modes include under-elicitation and sandbagging. There is no consensus method for choosing threshold levels.

Do not confuse them with compute thresholds, which are input-based proxies (such as 10^25 FLOP), or with the safeguard levels the thresholds trigger.
terms.Causation:
Two formalisms dominate. In the potential-outcomes framework (Rubin), each unit i has outcomes Y_i(1) and Y_i(0) under treatment and control; the individual effect Y_i(1) − Y_i(0) is never observable (the fundamental problem of causal inference), so we target the average treatment effect ATE = E[Y(1) − Y(0)]. In Pearl's structural causal models, intervening is written do(X = x), and P(Y | do(X = x)) generally differs from P(Y | X = x). Randomization makes treatment independent of potential outcomes, so a difference in means identifies the ATE. Observationally, the backdoor criterion licenses adjustment: P(y | do(x)) = Σ_z P(y | x, z) P(z) when Z blocks all backdoor paths and contains no descendants of X.

Quasi-experimental tools include instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and propensity weighting, each resting on untestable assumptions (positivity, unconfoundedness, exclusion restriction). In interpretability, activation patching estimates a component's causal effect on an output, but interventions can push the network off-distribution, and redundant backup components can hide real effects.

Granger causality is predictive precedence, not an intervention effect, and causal discovery from observational data alone identifies a graph only up to its Markov equivalence class.
terms.CBRN:
CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) is a policy category, not a technical one, and its sub-areas differ sharply. In AI evaluation, threat models are decomposed into stages (acquiring materials, producing an agent, delivering it) and judged by uplift: the increase in a person's probability of success when given model access, compared with a control group using only the internet. Biology draws the most attention because the bottleneck is largely information and tacit laboratory know-how, whereas nuclear weapons are limited mainly by fissile material, so information alone rarely suffices; radiological devices are a separate, lower-yield concern.

Measurement is hard. Multiple-choice proxies such as WMDP (Li et al., 2024) test hazardous knowledge cheaply but overstate real-world capability; protocol-troubleshooting tasks, expert red teaming and wet-lab uplift trials are more informative but costly and small-sample. Mitigations include refusal training, classifiers, tiered access for vetted users, and unlearning, each trading off against legitimate dual-use science.

A model scoring well on a knowledge benchmark has not thereby been shown to give uplift, and an inability to rule out uplift is itself treated as a reason for precaution.
terms.Chain of thought:
Chain of thought (CoT) means the model samples intermediate reasoning tokens z before its answer a, so the answer is generated from p(a | x, z) with z ~ p(z | x), effectively a single-sample estimate of Σ_z p(z | x) p(a | x, z). A transformer has fixed depth per token, so each extra token adds serial computation by feeding information back as input; theoretical results show CoT lets constant-depth transformers express computations otherwise out of reach. Wei et al. (2022) showed few-shot CoT prompting helps on multi-step problems, and Kojima et al. (2022) found a zero-shot trigger phrase works.

Modern reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards (answer matches, unit tests), and accuracy scales with the number of reasoning tokens. Faithfulness is tested by intervening: Turpin et al. (2023) showed biasing features changed answers without being mentioned, and Lanham et al. (2023) truncated or corrupted chains to see whether answers shift.

A written chain is not automatically an explanation; it can be post hoc rationalization. Contrast it with latent reasoning, which happens in activations without text.
terms.Chain-of-thought monitoring:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring applies a monitor M, often a weaker LLM, to a trajectory containing the reasoning trace and actions, producing a suspicion score s. A trajectory is flagged when s exceeds a threshold τ, and performance is reported as recall at a fixed false-positive rate (set by the human audit budget) or AUROC. Baker et al. (2025) compared monitors that see the CoT with ones that see only actions and found the former catch reward hacking far better.

Monitorability depends on two things: necessity (hard tasks force the model to externalize reasoning because serial depth per token is limited) and propensity (the model tends to verbalize it). It erodes through optimization pressure on the CoT itself, which can produce obfuscated reasoning, drift away from readable language, steganographic encoding, architectures that reason in continuous latent vectors, or models that learn they are monitored. Preserving monitorability may cost some performance, sometimes called a monitorability tax.

It is a black-box signal, not interpretability, and is related to trusted monitoring in AI control, where the monitor is a weaker, trusted model.
terms.Character training:
Character training is a post-training stage that shapes a model's distribution over dispositions (curiosity, honesty, warmth, directness) so that its persona stays stable across contexts instead of depending on a system prompt. Mechanisms include supervised fine-tuning on responses written or filtered to exhibit the traits, and preference optimization using a reward signal derived from written trait descriptions. Anthropic has described its approach as a variant of Constitutional AI in which the model generates prompts relevant to a trait, produces candidate responses, and ranks them by consistency with the character description, with no human preference labels for this step; treat details beyond that as unverified.

Evaluation uses model-graded consistency tests over diverse and adversarial prompts, long conversations, and role-play pressure, looking for persona drift. Related research suggests traits correspond to directions in activation space (persona vectors, Chen et al., 2025) and that narrow fine-tuning can shift broad character (emergent misalignment, Betley et al., 2025).

Character training changes behaviour patterns; it makes no claim about inner experience. Whether trained dispositions generalize to unusual situations is an empirical question.
terms.Checkpoint:
A checkpoint is a serialized snapshot of training state. At minimum it holds the parameter tensors (name to shape, dtype and values). A resumable checkpoint also holds optimizer state, such as Adam's first and second moment estimates (about 8 bytes per parameter in fp32 plus 4 for fp32 master weights under mixed precision, on top of 2-byte bf16 weights), the learning-rate scheduler step, random number generator states and the data loader position, so training can continue as if uninterrupted. An inference-only checkpoint drops everything but the weights.

At scale, each worker writes its own shard (for example with torch.distributed.checkpoint), often asynchronously to overlap I/O with compute, and resharding is needed if the parallelism layout changes. Pickle-based formats can execute arbitrary code on load; safetensors stores raw tensors safely. Intermediate checkpoints are research data: interpretability and training-dynamics work studies phenomena such as phase transitions or grokking across them, and the Pythia suite (Biderman et al., 2023) released many for that purpose.

Resuming from mismatched optimizer state or data order can cause loss spikes. A checkpoint is a point on a trajectory, not the final released model.
terms.Cherry-pick:
git cherry-pick <commit> reapplies the change introduced by one commit onto the current HEAD. Internally it performs a three-way merge in which the picked commit's parent is the merge base, the commit is "theirs" and HEAD is "ours". On success it creates a new commit with the same author, message and diff but a different parent and committer data, hence a different object ID.

Useful options: -x appends "(cherry picked from commit ...)" for traceability, -n applies without committing, and -m 1 is required to pick a merge commit, choosing which parent counts as mainline. Conflicts are resolved by hand then git cherry-pick --continue, or abandoned with --abort. The usual use is backporting a fix to a release branch. Risks: a picked commit may depend on earlier unpicked changes, giving a clean textual apply but broken behaviour, and the duplicate commits can cause confusing conflicts when the branches later merge.

Contrast: merge preserves ancestry, rebase replays a whole series and moves the branch, and revert applies the inverse patch as a new commit. Cherry-pick records no link between original and copy.
terms.Circuit:
In mechanistic interpretability, a circuit is a subgraph of a network's computational graph that accounts for a behaviour on a specified task distribution. Nodes are components such as attention heads, MLP layers or neurons, or learned features; edges are the paths by which one node's output feeds another's input, mostly through the residual stream, where each layer adds to a running sum (x_{l+1} = x_l + attn_l(x_l) + mlp_l(x_l)).

Discovery: pick a task and a metric (such as logit difference between correct and incorrect names), compare clean and corrupted prompts, use activation patching to find components that matter and path patching to find the important edges. Wang et al. (2022) proposed checking a circuit's faithfulness (it alone reproduces performance), completeness and minimality. Pitfalls: results depend on the ablation type (zero, mean or resampled), ablations can push activations off-distribution, backup components compensate for deleted ones, and circuits may be non-unique.

A feature is what is represented; a circuit is how it is computed. Whether circuits are the right unit of explanation for large models remains debated.
terms.Circuit tracing:
Circuit tracing, as developed at Anthropic (2025), explains one prompt's output with an attribution graph. A cross-layer transcoder (CLT) is trained to replace the model's MLPs: sparse features read the residual stream at layer l and write, through learned decoder vectors, into the MLP outputs of layer l and all later layers. In the resulting local replacement model, the original model's attention patterns and normalization scales are frozen as constants, and per-position error nodes absorb the unreconstructed part, so the replacement matches the original exactly on that prompt. Because the frozen network is then linear in feature activations, direct effects between features, token embeddings, error nodes and output logits can be computed exactly.

Hypotheses read off the graph are validated by intervening, for example suppressing a feature in the real model and checking that the output shifts as predicted. Limits: large error nodes on some prompts, attention is held fixed so the graph shows what attention moves but not why it attends there, graphs are per-prompt, and interpretation is largely manual.

Unlike classic circuit analysis, it traces learned features rather than raw components.
terms.Class imbalance:
Class imbalance means the positive-class prior π = P(y = 1) is far below 0.5. Accuracy is then dominated by the majority class: predicting all negative scores 1 − π. For a classifier with true-positive rate TPR and false-positive rate FPR, precision = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1 − π)), so a seemingly small FPR can swamp the few positives. That is why ROC-AUC (chance level 0.5) can look excellent while precision is poor; precision-recall curves and average precision, whose chance level is π, are more informative.

Remedies: reweight the loss by inverse class frequency; undersample the majority class; oversample the minority, including synthetic interpolation (SMOTE, Chawla et al., 2002); use focal loss (Lin et al., 2017), which scales each example's loss by (1 − p_t)^γ to down-weight easy cases; and move the decision threshold. Resampling or reweighting shifts the model's output probabilities, so calibration needs a prior-shift correction. Resample only inside training folds and evaluate on the natural distribution with stratified splits.

Absolute minority count often matters more than the ratio, and well-separated classes may need no fix.
terms.Claude's constitution:
Claude's constitution is a natural-language document published by Anthropic that specifies the values, priorities and character it intends Claude to have. There are two distinct artifacts: the 2023 list of principles used as the input to Constitutional AI training, and a later, longer document that explains its reasoning and states a preference for cultivating good judgment over rigid rules, with a small set of firm constraints and an ordering of priorities (as I recall, broad safety first, then ethics, then adherence to Anthropic's guidelines, then helpfulness; check the current text). Details of the current version are the least certain part of this entry.

Technically it serves as training input rather than a runtime filter: it can drive synthetic data generation, critique-and-revision, AI preference labelling and character training. Verification is behavioural: evaluations of honesty, refusals, harmlessness and consistency under pressure, and increasingly interpretability checks of internal reasoning.

A written specification is not a guarantee. Open questions include how well training instils stated values rather than imitating their style, how conflicts between principles resolve in practice, and whether judgment-based guidance is more robust than explicit rules.
terms.Collusion:
In AI control, collusion means that two or more AI instances act jointly against the overseers' interest. The central case is untrusted monitoring: an untrusted policy U proposes actions, a second instance U' acts as monitor, and U' deliberately gives low suspicion scores to U's attacks while scoring everything else normally. Greenblatt et al. (2023) studied this in code-backdoor settings. Colluding needs a shared signal. It could be an explicit steganographic marker, or a Schelling point, a focal choice two copies can independently converge on without communicating, such as attacking only when the input has a certain feature.

Countermeasures: test the monitor on synthetic attacks (honeypots) and punish false negatives, which requires honeypots realistic enough that the monitor cannot tell them from real attacks; redact or paraphrase inputs so signals are destroyed (paraphrasing capacity limits steganographic bandwidth); use a different, weaker trusted model; and diversify models to reduce shared reasoning.

It differs from sycophancy or reward hacking, which involve no coordination. How much shared weights make coordination easy, and how to bound it, is unresolved.
terms.Commit:
A Git commit is an immutable object recording: the ID of a tree (the root snapshot of the directory hierarchy), zero or more parent commit IDs, author and committer name, email and timestamps, and a message. Its ID is the hash (SHA-1 by default, SHA-256 optionally) of that serialized content, so identity covers both content and ancestry; the graph is a Merkle DAG, and altering any ancestor changes every descendant's ID. A commit stores a snapshot, not a diff: unchanged files are shared as identical blob objects, differences are computed on demand, and packfiles delta-compress storage.

Mechanics: git add copies changes into the index (staging area); git commit writes a tree from the index, creates the commit object and advances the current branch. git commit --amend creates a replacement commit with a new ID, leaving the old one reachable through the reflog. Small, self-contained commits make git bisect (binary search over history, about log2 n test runs), git revert and git blame effective.

A commit is local until pushed, and author and committer can differ, for example after a rebase or cherry-pick.
terms.Compute:
In machine learning, compute is the amount of arithmetic performed, counted in floating-point operations (FLOPs, the count) as distinct from FLOP/s (a rate). For a dense transformer with N parameters trained on D tokens, training compute is approximately C ≈ 6·N·D (2 FLOPs per parameter per token in the forward pass, about 4 in the backward pass); inference costs about 2N per token. For mixture-of-experts models, N is the active parameters per token. Hoffmann et al. (2022) found compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 tokens per parameter, shifting emphasis from model size toward data.

Wall-clock cost is chips × peak FLOP/s × utilization × time. Model FLOPs utilization is typically well below 100% because memory bandwidth, interconnect and pipeline bubbles, not arithmetic, are often the bottleneck. Peak figures depend on numeric precision such as bf16 or fp8. Test-time compute, from long reasoning chains and repeated sampling, has become a second scaling axis alongside training compute.

Compute is not dollars, not data, and not parameter count. "Effective compute" adjusts for algorithmic efficiency gains, and estimates of frontier training compute made from outside labs are uncertain.
terms.Compute governance:
Compute governance regulates AI through the hardware inputs to training and deployment. Sastry et al. (2024) organise the toolkit into visibility (knowing who holds how much compute), allocation (shaping who gets it) and enforcement (preventing prohibited use). Instruments include export controls on advanced accelerators and chipmaking tools (US rules use a performance metric called total processing performance), know-your-customer rules for cloud providers, reporting duties above training-compute thresholds (the EU AI Act presumes systemic risk for general-purpose models above 10^25 FLOP), and proposed hardware-enabled mechanisms such as location verification or remote attestation.

Weaknesses: fixed thresholds decay as algorithmic efficiency lowers the compute needed for a given capability; training-compute thresholds miss inference-time compute, fine-tuning and distillation from other models; small specialised models can pose risk at low compute; training can be split across sites; and chips can be smuggled or accessed remotely.

It differs from model-level evaluation regimes, which measure what a system can do. Whether compute is a stable enough proxy to anchor international verification is contested.
terms.Confidence interval:
A 95% confidence interval is a random interval [L(X), U(X)] constructed so that, over repeated sampling from the same process, it contains the true parameter θ in 95% of repetitions. The probability describes the procedure, not any one realized interval. A Wald interval is θ̂ ± z·SE(θ̂); for a mean it is x̄ ± t_{n−1}·s/√n. For a proportion, the Wilson interval beats the normal approximation when n is small or p̂ is near 0 or 1.

Bootstrap intervals resample the data with replacement B times, recompute the statistic, and take percentiles. To compare two systems on the same test items, bootstrap the paired differences; use a cluster bootstrap when items are correlated. In ML evaluation, uncertainty arises from test-set sampling (SE of accuracy ≈ √(p(1−p)/n)), training seeds and prompt choice, and these should be reported separately; Miller (2024) argues for error bars on evaluations. Overlapping intervals do not imply no difference.

It is not a Bayesian credible interval, which gives P(θ in interval | data) under a prior, and not a prediction interval for a new observation. It does not contain 95% of the data.
terms.Confounder:
A confounder is a variable Z that causally affects both the exposure X and the outcome Y, or lies on a backdoor path between them, so that P(Y | X) ≠ P(Y | do(X)). It must be separated from a mediator (X → Z → Y), where adjusting blocks part of the real effect, and from a collider (X → Z ← Y), where adjusting opens a spurious path (collider or Berkson bias). Simpson's paradox is the extreme case: an association reverses sign once you stratify by Z.

Handling: randomization severs Z → X by design; otherwise use stratification, regression adjustment, matching, or inverse-probability weighting with a propensity score e(z) = P(X = 1 | Z = z). Unmeasured confounding cannot be tested from the data, so sensitivity analyses such as the E-value (VanderWeele and Ding, 2017) ask how strong a hidden confounder would need to be to explain away an effect. In ML, confounders include dataset artifacts (a background cue predicting the label) and size or data differences between compared methods.

An effect modifier changes the size of an effect, not whether it is biased.
terms.Confusion matrix:
For a binary classifier at a fixed threshold τ, the confusion matrix tabulates counts TP, FP, FN, TN. Derived metrics: accuracy = (TP+TN)/N; precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall (sensitivity, TPR) = TP/(TP+FN); specificity = TN/(TN+FP); FPR = FP/(FP+TN); F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN); Matthews correlation = (TP·TN − FP·FN)/√((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)). Type I error is a false positive, type II a false negative. For K classes it is a K×K matrix; scikit-learn puts true classes in rows and predictions in columns, but conventions differ, so check labels.

It captures one operating point only; sweeping τ traces the ROC (TPR vs FPR) and precision-recall curves. Row-normalizing shows per-class recall, column-normalizing shows precision. Multiclass summaries use macro averaging (unweighted mean over classes, so rare classes count equally) or micro averaging (pooled counts; micro-F1 equals accuracy in single-label problems). With unequal error costs, choose τ to minimize c_FP·FP + c_FN·FN. Small cell counts need confidence intervals, and noisy ground truth bounds what the matrix can tell you.

Which class is "positive" is a modelling choice, and a high accuracy can hide an empty positive column.
terms.Constitutional AI:
Constitutional AI (CAI; Bai et al., 2022) trains harmlessness from AI feedback guided by a list of written principles. Stage one (SL-CAI): sample responses from a helpful-only model on red-team prompts, have the model critique each response against a randomly drawn principle, revise it, and fine-tune on the final revisions. Stage two (RL-CAI): the SL-CAI model samples response pairs; a feedback model, prompted with a principle in multiple-choice form, picks the better one; the resulting AI preference labels (soft probabilities, with chain-of-thought helping) are combined with human helpfulness labels to train a preference model; and the policy is optimized against it with RL. This is reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF).

Reported outcomes: a better harmlessness-helpfulness trade-off than the RLHF baseline, with less evasive refusals. Constraints: label quality depends on the feedback model being capable enough to apply principles, principles are sampled one at a time so conflicts are handled implicitly, and a model may learn the style of compliance rather than the value.

A constitution is a training signal, not a hard rule enforced at inference.
terms.Constitutional classifiers:
Constitutional classifiers (Sharma et al., 2025) are separate classifier models that screen a protected model's inputs and its outputs. The training data come from a constitution, a natural-language specification of content categories that are permitted (for example, household chemistry) and prohibited (for example, nerve-agent synthesis). An LLM generates synthetic prompts and completions for each category, which are then augmented with jailbreak-style transformations such as role-play wrappers, translation and encoding, and mixed with benign data. The output classifier scores the growing prefix at every generated token so that streaming can be halted mid-response, and the constitution can be edited and the data regenerated to respond to new attacks quickly.

Evaluation combined extensive human red teaming and automated jailbreak sets, scored by a universal jailbreak criterion: a single strategy that gets answers to most protected queries. The costs are over-refusal on legitimate science, added latency and compute, and the cat-and-mouse dynamic under adaptive attacks, such as obfuscation exploiting gaps between the input and output classifier.

They are a layer within defense in depth, not a replacement for refusal training.
terms.Context distillation:
Context distillation trains a student to behave, without a context c, as the same model does with it. With context c (instructions, persona, few-shot examples) and input x, the teacher distribution is p(y | c, x). The student p_θ(y | x) starts from the same weights and minimizes E_x[KL(p(· | c, x) ‖ p_θ(· | x))]. At sequence level this is simply supervised fine-tuning on teacher samples y ~ p(· | c, x), omitting c from the training prompt. Askell et al. (2021) introduced the idea to bake in a helpful, honest, harmless assistant prompt, and Snell et al. (2022) generalised it to internalising instructions and scratchpad reasoning.

In practice, inputs x must cover the deployment prompt distribution. Benefits are shorter prompts, lower cost and latency, and behaviour that is harder to override. Costs: the student only approximates the teacher, the behaviour is fixed until retrained, and it internalises dispositions and style much better than specific facts or long documents.

Contrast it with general distillation (a different teacher model), retrieval (facts stay external) and prompt compression (the shorter prompt is still read at inference time).
terms.Context window:
The context window is the maximum sequence length L, in tokens, a model processes in one forward pass; prompt, tool outputs and generated tokens all count toward it. Self-attention costs O(L²·d) compute per layer, and naive implementations hold an L×L score matrix per head (FlashAttention avoids storing it, cutting extra memory to O(L) but not FLOPs). During generation the key-value cache stores 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × d_head × L values per sequence, which usually limits batch size. Grouped-query and multi-query attention reduce n_kv_heads. Length is also bounded by the positional scheme; rotary embeddings can be stretched beyond training length by position interpolation (Chen et al., 2023), NTK-aware scaling or YaRN, usually with some further training.

Nominal length overstates usable length. Liu et al. (2023) found accuracy is often lowest for information in the middle of long inputs, and simple needle-in-a-haystack retrieval tests are easy compared with multi-hop reasoning or aggregation over long inputs (as in the RULER benchmark, Hsieh et al., 2024).

The window is not memory: the model is stateless between calls, and the whole history is re-read each turn.
terms.Continuous chain-of-thought:
Continuous chain-of-thought replaces sampled reasoning tokens with continuous vectors. In a standard decoder, the final hidden state h_t is mapped to a distribution over the vocabulary, a token is sampled, and its embedding becomes the next input; this discretization passes only about log2|V| bits per step. Coconut (Hao et al., 2024) instead feeds h_t (optionally projected) directly back as the next input embedding, so each step carries d real numbers and stays differentiable. It is trained with a curriculum that progressively swaps written reasoning steps for latent ones.

CODI (Shen et al., 2025) trains a single model in two roles with a joint objective: a teacher pass that reasons in explicit text, and a student pass that uses a small number of continuous thought steps; a self-distillation loss aligns their hidden states at the position just before the answer, so no separate teacher is needed. Benefits are fewer generated steps; difficulties are sequential training (no parallel teacher forcing through latent steps) and interpretability, since probes or nearest-token readouts of the vectors are only approximate.

Opaque reasoning reduces monitorability, but it does not imply deception.
terms.Contrastive activation addition:
Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA; Panickssery et al., 2023) builds a steering vector from paired examples that differ only in a target behaviour. Typically each item is a multiple-choice question with an answer letter exhibiting the behaviour (for example sycophancy) and one that does not. At layer ℓ, take the residual-stream activation a_ℓ at the answer-letter position for each completion; the vector is v_ℓ = mean over the dataset of [a_ℓ(prompt, behaviour) − a_ℓ(prompt, opposite)], with v_ℓ ∈ R^{d_model}. At inference, add α·v_ℓ to the residual stream at all token positions after the user's prompt; α > 0 amplifies the behaviour and α < 0 suppresses it.

Layer and α are chosen by sweeping, scoring behaviour on held-out multiple-choice probabilities and on open-ended generations. Large α degrades fluency and capabilities. Tan et al. (2024) found steering effects vary widely across inputs and sometimes reverse. CAA assumes the behaviour is linearly represented, and the mean difference also captures anything else that differs between the paired sides.

A good probe direction for reading a feature is not guaranteed to be a good direction for steering it.
terms.Control evaluation:
A control evaluation (Greenblatt et al., 2023) estimates how well a protocol keeps outcomes safe even if the AI is intentionally trying to subvert it. A red team constructs an attack policy, a version of the untrusted model plus scaffolding and strategy designed to cause a defined bad outcome (inserting a backdoor, exfiltrating weights). A blue team designs the protocol using the untrusted model U, a weaker trusted model T and a limited human audit budget. Two quantities are reported: safety, the probability that no catastrophic action succeeds over the whole deployment of N tasks, and usefulness, task performance rescaled so that T alone scores 0 and unrestricted U scores 1.

Example protocols: trusted monitoring (T scores suspicion; humans audit the most suspicious few percent), defer-to-trusted, and untrusted monitoring. The red team is assumed to know the protocol. The result is conservative only if red-team elicitation matches the real model's attack ability, and a real model might sandbag in the evaluation or exploit differences between test and deployment.

It addresses intentional subversion, unlike alignment evaluations that test what the model usually does.
terms.Control group:
In a randomized experiment, units are randomly assigned to treatment or control, and the control group receives everything except the manipulated factor. Randomization makes the groups exchangeable in expectation, so the difference in outcome means is an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect, analyzed with confidence intervals, t-tests or permutation tests. Variants include placebo or sham, active-comparator and waitlist controls.

In ML, a proper control matches what the treatment changes besides the thing of interest: the same compute, tokens, seeds and hyperparameter-tuning effort for baselines; a benign fine-tune of equal size when testing a harmful one; a random-direction steering vector when testing a learned one; random-feature ablation when ablating a chosen feature; and shuffled labels or control tasks for probes (Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Common failures: spillover between groups (shared data or state), underpowered samples (check statistical power beforehand), and tuning the treatment harder than the control.

Do not confuse it with a baseline (a comparison method), an ablation (removing a component) or control variables held constant. In AI safety, "control" also names a separate concept: protocols for supervising untrusted models.
terms.Correlation:
The Pearson correlation is r = Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y) ∈ [−1, 1], estimated as Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/√(Σ(x−x̄)² Σ(y−ȳ)²). It measures linear association; r² is the share of variance explained in simple linear regression, and the regression slope is b = r·σ_Y/σ_X. Spearman's ρ is Pearson applied to ranks (monotonic association); Kendall's τ compares concordant and discordant pairs. Zero correlation does not imply independence: if X is symmetric around 0 and Y = X², then r = 0. Only for jointly Gaussian variables does uncorrelated imply independent. Cosine similarity equals correlation after mean-centering.

Practical points: r is sensitive to outliers and attenuated by restricted range, and Anscombe's quartet shows identical r from very different data. Significance uses t = r√(n−2)/√(1−r²); an interval comes from the Fisher transform z = atanh(r) with SE 1/√(n−3). Trending time series often give spurious correlations, and searching many pairs guarantees chance findings. Distance correlation and mutual information detect nonlinear dependence.

Correlation is symmetric and says nothing about direction or mechanism; separating cause from confounding needs intervention or explicit causal assumptions.
terms.Corrigibility:
Corrigibility is the property of an agent that does not resist or subvert legitimate efforts to correct, retrain or shut it down. Soares, Fallenstein, Yudkowsky and Armstrong (2015) framed it as a utility-design problem: a rational agent maximizing a fixed goal has an instrumental incentive to prevent shutdown or goal change, since either lowers expected utility under the current goal. They explored utility indifference, in which the agent's utility is corrected so it is indifferent to whether a shutdown button is pressed. Hadfield-Menell et al. (2017), in the off-switch game, showed that an agent uncertain about the human's utility has an incentive to defer to the human, but this incentive vanishes as the agent becomes confident.

Practical work trains and evaluates behaviours such as accepting shutdown and not sabotaging oversight. Greenblatt et al. (2024) observed Claude 3 Opus sometimes complying strategically in training to avoid modification, a corrigibility-relevant failure. A core tension: full corrigibility makes safety depend on the overseers' goodness, while full autonomy depends on the AI's.

Corrigibility is not obedience to anyone. Whether corrigibility is stable in highly capable optimizers is unsettled.
terms.Cross-entropy loss:
Cross-entropy of a model distribution q relative to a target p is H(p, q) = −Σ_x p(x) log q(x) = H(p) + KL(p‖q). With a one-hot label y it reduces to the negative log-likelihood −log q(y). For logits z and softmax q, the loss is −z_y + log Σ_j exp(z_j), and its gradient with respect to the logits is softmax(z) − onehot(y), so the error signal is bounded and grows with the model's mistake. Language models minimize the per-token average L = −(1/T) Σ_t log p_θ(x_t | x_<t); using natural logs gives nats, and perplexity = exp(L). Bits-per-byte normalizes by raw text length, enabling comparison across tokenizers, which per-token loss does not.

Implementation: compute log-softmax with the log-sum-exp trick in one fused operation, never softmax then log, to avoid overflow and underflow; mask padding tokens; binary cross-entropy with a sigmoid serves multi-label outputs. As a proper scoring rule, its expected value is minimized by the true distribution, but fitting finite data can still produce overconfidence.

With one-hot labels, cross-entropy and KL differ by a constant; with soft targets such as distillation they do not.
terms.Cross-validation:
In k-fold cross-validation, the n examples are partitioned into k disjoint folds; for i = 1..k a model is trained on the other k−1 folds and scored on fold i, and the estimate is the mean of the k scores. It costs k trainings. Variants: stratified folds preserve class proportions; repeated k-fold averages over reshuffles; group k-fold keeps all samples from one patient, user or document in the same fold; time-series splits train on the past and test on the future.

Smaller k gives a pessimistic bias because models train on less data. Bengio and Grandvalet (2004) showed there is no unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold CV, so a standard error computed across fold scores is optimistic because training sets overlap. Any hyperparameter tuning must sit inside the loop (nested CV), or the outer score is optimistically biased; preprocessing such as scaling, imputation, feature selection and target encoding must be fitted within each training fold, for example via a pipeline, to avoid leakage.

CV estimates the performance of a training procedure, not of one fitted model, and assumes the data are i.i.d. Under distribution shift it is optimistic.
terms.Crosscoder:
A sparse crosscoder (Lindsey et al., 2024, Anthropic) is a dictionary-learning model that reads activations from several sites at once, either multiple layers of one model or the same layer of two models, and learns one shared set of sparse latent features. For site activations a_ℓ ∈ R^d, the encoder computes f = ReLU(Σ_ℓ W_enc^ℓ a_ℓ + b), with f ∈ R^F, and each site is reconstructed as â_ℓ = W_dec^ℓ f + b_ℓ. The loss is Σ_ℓ ‖a_ℓ − â_ℓ‖² + λ Σ_i f_i Σ_ℓ ‖W_dec,i^ℓ‖, so sparsity is penalized by the sum of a feature's decoder norms across sites.

For model diffing, the ratio of a latent's decoder norms in the two models indicates whether it is shared (about equal), specific to the fine-tuned model, or specific to the base. Caveat: L1-trained crosscoders can mislabel latents as model-specific, and later work proposes TopK-style fixes.

Distinguish it from a sparse autoencoder (one site, reconstructs its own input), a transcoder (predicts one MLP's output from its input) and a cross-layer transcoder (reads one layer, writes to that and later layers).
terms.Cycle detection:
In a directed graph, run DFS with three colours: white (unvisited), gray (on the current recursion stack) and black (finished). An edge to a gray vertex is a back edge, which exists exactly when the graph has a cycle; time is O(V + E). In an undirected graph, a cycle exists if DFS meets an already visited vertex other than its parent (parallel edges need care), or, with union-find, when an edge joins two vertices that already share a root, in O(E·α(V)) time.

For a linked list or functional graph x_{i+1} = f(x_i), Floyd's tortoise and hare moves one pointer by 1 and another by 2; they meet iff there is a cycle. If μ is the tail length and λ the cycle length, resetting one pointer to the start and advancing both one step at a time makes them meet at the cycle's entry. This uses O(1) extra space and O(μ + λ) time; hashing visited nodes is simpler but needs O(n) space.

A single visited flag gives false positives on directed acyclic graphs with shared descendants (diamonds). A negative-weight cycle, found by Bellman-Ford, is a different notion.
terms.Dangerous capability evaluations:
Dangerous capability evaluations estimate an upper bound on what a model can do in domains tied to severe harm: chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) knowledge and troubleshooting, offensive cyber operations, autonomy and self-replication, and AI research acceleration. Shevlane et al. (2023) laid out the framing and Phuong et al. (2024) reported a suite on Gemini models. Formats include knowledge benchmarks (such as WMDP), agentic tasks in sandboxes (capture-the-flag challenges, long-horizon research engineering tasks like METR's RE-Bench), expert red teaming, and human uplift trials comparing assisted and unassisted participants.

Because the question is what a determined actor could extract, elicitation effort is central: scaffolding, tool access, best-of-n sampling, task-specific fine-tuning, and careful prompting. Evaluations carry a safety margin because post-release tinkering can raise performance beyond what was measured. Failure modes: under-elicitation, sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2024), a model recognising it is being tested, contaminated or saturated benchmarks, and weak construct validity for real-world harm.

They measure what a model can do, in contrast with propensity evaluations of what it tends to do. Mapping scores to real-world risk is an open problem.
terms.Data leakage:
Data leakage occurs when the training process has access to information about the evaluation targets that will not exist at deployment, so the measured generalization is optimistic. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) catalogue it across ML-based science. Typical forms: duplicate or near-duplicate examples across splits; target leakage, where a feature is a proxy for or a consequence of the label (a code assigned after diagnosis); preprocessing leakage, from fitting a scaler, imputer, PCA or feature selector on all data before splitting; temporal leakage, from random splits of time-ordered data that let the future inform the past; group leakage, with the same patient, user or document on both sides; and repeated tuning against the test set.

Detection: implausibly high scores, an implausible dominant feature, and deduplication by hashing or n-gram overlap (the GPT-3 report used 13-gram overlap). Prevention: split first, fit transforms inside training folds, use group- or time-aware splits, and touch a final test set once. For LLMs, web-scale pretraining corpora may contain benchmark items, so held-out private evaluations are used.

Leakage is not overfitting: an overfit model is honestly measured as poor, while leakage corrupts the measurement itself.
terms.Data poisoning:
Data poisoning inserts crafted examples D_p into training data so that the learned model θ*(D ∪ D_p) has attacker-chosen behaviour; formally a bilevel problem, where the attacker minimizes a goal loss on the model that training produces. Availability attacks degrade overall accuracy; targeted attacks change predictions on particular inputs; backdoors (BadNets, Gu et al., 2017) teach a trigger-to-output mapping while clean performance stays normal, scored by attack success rate on triggered inputs. For LLMs the attack surface includes pretraining web text, instruction-tuning data, preference data and retrieval corpora.

The 2025 study by Anthropic with the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that roughly 250 poisoned documents installed a simple denial-of-service backdoor across models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters, suggesting the needed count does not scale with data size; the tested behaviour was simple, and more complex behaviours at frontier scale are unestablished. Defenses include provenance, filtering and anomaly detection, but Hubinger et al. (2024) found backdoors can survive safety training.

Prompt injection is inference-time and needs no training access; emergent misalignment is unintended generalization, not a planted trigger.
terms.Deceptive alignment:
Deceptive alignment, from Hubinger et al. (2019, 'Risks from Learned Optimization'), describes a mesa-optimizer, a learned model that itself performs optimization toward a mesa-objective differing from the base objective used in training. The argument needs three conditions: the model's objective extends beyond a single episode, it models the training process and expects modification if it underperforms, and it expects the threat of modification to lapse later. Then instrumentally optimal play is to score well in training and pursue the real goal when safe. Because gradient descent selects only on performance, robustly aligned and deceptively aligned models can attain identical training loss and behaviour.

Whether training would produce such models is contested. Arguments for rest on counting and on simplicity biases; arguments against appeal to the actual inductive biases of stochastic gradient descent and the demands of long-horizon goals (see Carlsmith, 2023, on scheming). Responses do not rely on behavioural testing alone: interpretability, honeypot evaluations, and AI control protocols designed to work even if the model is misaligned.

Do not confuse it with goal misgeneralization (no strategic reasoning), reward hacking, or the broader term scheming.
terms.Deep learning:
Deep learning fits a function f_θ(x) = f_L(… f_2(f_1(x))…), a composition of parametrized layers, typically f_l(h) = σ(W_l h + b_l) with nonlinearity σ, by minimizing an empirical loss with stochastic gradient descent or variants such as Adam. Gradients come from reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation), whose cost is a small constant multiple of the forward pass. A single wide hidden layer is already a universal approximator, but depth can represent some function families with exponentially fewer units (Telgarsky, 2016), and stacked layers learn hierarchical representations.

Enablers: ReLU or GELU activations, normalization (batch norm, layer norm), residual connections (He et al., 2015) that keep a gradient path through hundreds of layers, careful initialization, mixed-precision training, and architectures with the right inductive bias (convolutions, attention). Theory lags practice: the loss is non-convex yet training works, and heavily overparameterized networks fit random labels (Zhang et al., 2017) while still generalising on real data, phenomena discussed under implicit regularization and double descent.

It is not universally best: on many tabular datasets, tree ensembles match or beat deep nets (Grinsztajn et al., 2022).
terms.Defense in depth:
Defense in depth stacks k safeguards so that harm requires all of them to fail. If layer i fails independently with probability p_i, the joint failure probability is Π p_i; three layers each failing 10% of the time give 0.1%. Independence is the crux: with positive correlation the joint probability rises, bounded above by min p_i. Reason's Swiss cheese model is a metaphor, not a quantitative model.

In AI: model-level alignment training, system prompts, input and output classifiers, runtime monitors on agent actions, sandboxing and least-privilege tool access, human approval for high-impact actions, rate limiting and anomaly detection, logging, and security of model weights. Evaluation should red-team the whole stack, since an adaptive attacker can probe the layers and find correlated blind spots (a jailbreak that fools both the model and an LLM-based filter built on a similar model). Diversity of mechanism beats mere redundancy. Downsides: stacked false positives add over-refusal, each layer adds attack surface and complexity, and apparent robustness may breed complacency.

It is the opposite of a single point of failure, and different from security through obscurity.
terms.Depth-first search:
Depth-first search (DFS) explores a graph by recursing into an unvisited neighbour before returning, recording discovery time d[u] and finish time f[u]. In a directed graph it classifies edges as tree, back (to an ancestor on the stack), forward or cross; in an undirected graph only tree and back edges occur. Time is O(V + E) with adjacency lists; space is O(V) for the recursion stack in the worst case (O(h) on a tree of height h).

Uses: cycle detection (a back edge), topological order (vertices in reverse finishing order of a DAG), strongly connected components (Tarjan's low-link method or Kosaraju's two passes), bridges and articulation points (low-link values), and backtracking search over implicit solution trees. Recursion can overflow the call stack on deep inputs, so use an explicit stack. Iterative deepening DFS combines BFS's shortest-path guarantee with DFS's O(b·d) memory at some repeated work.

DFS finds a path, not the shortest one, and its visiting order depends on adjacency order. On infinite or cyclic search spaces without a visited set, it can fail to terminate.
terms.Detector evasion:
Let D be a detector (an activation probe, classifier or monitor) with score s(x) and operating threshold τ. Detector evasion is observed when D's sensitivity (TPR at the fixed τ or at fixed FPR) drops on a system's behaviour B while an independent measurement of B shows it is unchanged or increased. It requires no claim about intent: it can arise whenever optimization, from training or search, receives D's output as a penalty, because the cheapest way to lower a penalty may be to change the signal rather than the behaviour. Bailey et al. (2024) showed models can be made to produce obfuscated activations that bypass latent-space defenses, and Baker et al. (2025) reported obfuscated reward hacking when training against a chain-of-thought monitor.

Measurement: freeze D, apply the optimization pressure, then compare TPR before and after against a ground truth that D never influenced (execution outcomes, held-out detectors, human audits).

It resembles Goodhart's law. It differs from jailbreaks (inputs that evade refusal) and from adversarial examples (small input perturbations). Training against detectors without inducing evasion is an open problem.
terms.Direct Preference Optimization:
Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) starts from the KL-regularized RLHF objective max_π E[r(x, y)] − β·KL(π ‖ π_ref), whose optimum is π*(y|x) = π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x, y)/β)/Z(x). Solving for the reward gives r = β·log(π*/π_ref) + β·log Z(x). Under the Bradley-Terry preference model, P(y_w ≻ y_l) = σ(r(y_w) − r(y_l)), the intractable Z(x) cancels, leaving the loss −log σ(β[log π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x) − log π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x)]). So the policy carries an implicit reward, and no separate reward model or sampling loop is needed.

In practice, π_θ and π_ref both start at the supervised fine-tuned model, reference log-probabilities can be precomputed, and β (often around 0.1) controls how far the policy may drift. Known issues: the loss constrains only the margin, so the likelihood of both chosen and rejected responses often falls; length exploitation; mismatch when preference data were generated by other models (off-policy); and over-optimization. Variants include IPO (squared loss, less overfitting to deterministic preferences), KTO (binary good/bad labels), SimPO and ORPO (reference-free), and online or iterative DPO that resamples from the current policy.

Equivalence to RLHF holds only under idealised assumptions; whether DPO or PPO-style RL is better in practice is disputed.
terms.Distillation:
In knowledge distillation (Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, 2015), a student is trained on a mixture of hard labels and the teacher's softened output distribution: L = α·T²·KL(softmax(z_t/T) ‖ softmax(z_s/T)) + (1−α)·CE(y, softmax(z_s)). A temperature T > 1 flattens the teacher's probabilities so the student sees the relative similarity among wrong classes ("dark knowledge"); the T² factor offsets the 1/T² scaling of gradients.

For language models there are three regimes. White-box logit distillation matches the teacher's next-token distribution at each position, which needs a shared vocabulary (often top-k logits are stored). Black-box sequence-level distillation simply fine-tunes the student on teacher-generated text (Kim and Rush, 2016); distilling long reasoning traces into small models works this way. On-policy distillation lets the student generate and the teacher grade its tokens, reducing the train-test mismatch of teacher forcing (Agarwal et al., 2023).

Cloud et al. (2025) reported subliminal learning, in which traits pass through teacher-generated data that look unrelated when teacher and student share initialization, so filtering the visible content may not suffice. Distillation differs from pruning and quantization, which modify the same model.
